stem: Which statement most precisely describes what a language model computes?
options: The most relevant document for a query
A parse tree for the sentence
A probability for every possible next token, given the text so far
A lookup of facts in a knowledge base
explanation: That is the whole contract: text so far → distribution over the next token. Everything else — chat, tools, reasoning — is built by running it in a loop.

stem: How does a model produce a 300-token answer?
options: In one forward pass that emits all 300 tokens at once
By retrieving a 300-token passage and editing it
By running the next-token prediction about 300 times, appending each pick to the input
By planning the whole answer, then writing it
explanation: Generation is autoregressive: predict, pick, append, repeat. Each new token conditions on all the earlier ones.

stem: A model confidently invents a function that does not exist in a library. What is the most accurate description?
options: A sampling error that temperature 0 eliminates
Evidence the model was trained on the wrong library
The mechanism working as designed on an input it had no grounds for — the most plausible continuation was produced
A rare bug that a stronger instruction will prevent
explanation: Next-token prediction produces plausible text whether or not grounds exist. Fixes live outside the model: real docs in the prompt, a tool that checks symbols, verification.

stem: In the example, greedy decoding (always the top token) produced 'the model reads the model reads…'. Why?
options: The corpus contained that exact sentence
Bigram models cannot represent sentence ends
The model ran out of context window
With no randomness, any repeated state repeats forever — greedy decoding has no source of variety
explanation: Greedy decoding is deterministic given the state; once the loop revisits a state it cycles. This is why real systems sample (Lesson 2.7).

stem: Your assistant made up a refund policy. In the loop diagram, where does the fix most likely belong?
options: The tokeniser — the policy was tokenised badly
The sampler — set temperature to 0
The model — ask it more firmly to be accurate
Your code — the real policy was not in the prompt and nothing verified the answer
explanation: Facts you care about must be in the prompt (retrieval) or checked afterwards. Instructions steer; they do not supply knowledge.

stem: Why can rewording a prompt change the answer substantially?
options: It cannot — only temperature changes answers
The prompt is the model's only input; any change alters the distribution over next tokens
Rewording changes the model's weights
The model caches previous prompts and compares them
explanation: Nothing else feeds the function. Wording, order and formatting all shift the distribution — sometimes a lot.

stem: Between two API calls, what does the model remember about the first?
options: Nothing — any 'memory' is history your code re-sends in the next prompt
Everything, for 24 hours
The last 10 messages
A summary it stores internally
explanation: The function's input is the prompt. State across calls is an application concern (Lesson 2.4, 2.5).

stem: Why is 'I don't know' unreliable from a plain LLM?
options: Models are forbidden from refusing
The vocabulary has no token for uncertainty
Nothing in next-token prediction represents the absence of knowledge; declining is itself just a learned continuation
Refusals are removed by top-p sampling
explanation: There is no first-class knowledge check. Give it a structured way to decline and verify the rest (Lessons 2.6, 2.8).

stem: Which component decides *which* token is emitted from the distribution?
options: The tokeniser
The sampler
The retriever
The embedding layer
explanation: The model proposes a distribution; the sampler picks. Temperature and top-p are sampler settings (Lesson 2.7).

stem: You want to reduce made-up answers in a product Q&A feature. Which change is most effective?
options: Add 'do not hallucinate' to the system prompt
Increase max_tokens so it can explain more
Lower the temperature to 0
Put the relevant product documents in the prompt and require citations
explanation: Move the facts from the model's memory into the prompt (RAG) and make answers checkable. Instructions and sampler settings only nudge.
